other_side: Zitron got to 'loops' first, predicting weeks earlier that the industry would push them — language models prompting language models, left to their token-hungry devices — as a desperate way to make users burn more compute and manufacture revenue. He notes the same Claude Code chief NLW quotes, Boris Cherny, is by his employer's arrangement 'allowed to burn upwards of $130,000 a month in tokens.' His wider case: loops, skills and 'software factories' are not progress but the rituals of 'the largest cargo cult of all time' — a tech industry out of ideas, copying the shape of past success and mistaking it for the substance. So eavesdropping on engineers buys not a six-month head start on the future but a front-row seat to token-burning theatre.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether the new engineering fashions — loops, skills, software factories — produce durable work output or merely more token consumption. Both accept the facts: engineers really are adopting these patterns and usage is climbing fast. The empirical question that will resolve is whether structured autonomy lifts measurable output per worker or only compute spend; the observable that settles it is independent, non-vendor productivity data — do teams working with loops and skills ship more with less rework, or just pay more per seat? The residue is pure worldview: early literacy of a real shift, or ritual imitation by an industry out of ideas. NLW is vindicated if encoded skills and loops yield durable gains and early adopters genuinely got ahead; Zitron if the practices mostly generate slop and quiet abandonment once subsidies tighten. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW sells head-start optimism to builders, Zitron sells cargo-cult certainty to sceptics — so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: undisciplined autonomy creates slop. Watch the first independent study of loop-and-skills workflows, and whether the practice survives tighter token limits.
